Chapter 1: The Clock and Mug

Tick Tick Tick. The seconds audibly passed through the routine of Gary and Gerty Hanover in the days before life came calling. The grandfather clock chimes had stopped working years ago, but that was of little concern to the occupants of the house. On rare occasions that the chimes attempted to sound, it startled those who were seated below the clock in the paisley-patterned wingback chairs. At those moments, the clock’s gears would grind and scrape along the edges of each other. A minor adjustment would remedy this interruption entirely, but the infrequency of the event was seen as remedy enough. A cherry end table sat between the two chairs. It supported a single lamp and two identical coffee mugs. The mugs had wider bases than necks. This served to keep the coffee hotter, longer. A piece of information that Gerty's university philosophy professor had imparted on her some 45 years earlier.
"It absolutely works, Gary. I would not continue to believe it if I had not tested it for many years." Gerty was always explaining and defending the benefits of the narrow-necked mugs to Gary. He had questioned the validity of the claim once, 40 years before. That conversation ended with his tossing and turning on the couch that night, so he had kept his mouth shut about it since then. However, he had never come out in agreement, thus Gerty felt it necessary to keep up the good fight. She asserted the claim about once every week or about once every six books read, depending on the length of the text.
Gary had decided to play it a little differently today. Forty years was a good run after all. He wondered what might happen if he changed his response. He enjoyed getting her dander up, but never wanted to ruffle her too much. That could be dangerous.
"How do you suppose it works, Gerty?" he asked with a tone of honest inquiry. Gerty had returned to her book after stating the claim. She was now in another world, Narnia to be precise. C.S. Lewis was one of her favorite authors and Narnia one of her favorite places. Gary could tell that Gerty was off, but he wanted to continue in his venture. He picked up his mug and slurped some of the hot coffee.
The slurping seemed to bring Gerty back to her wingback chair that sat by the malfunctioning grandfather clock, in front of the fireplace in the den of their home on Hanover Lane where they had lived for the past forty years. "What is it, Gary?" she asked as she placed her index finger on the page to hold her spot. Although it would not matter where she picked up because she had read this book numerous times before. She looked over at Gary above the rim of her reading glasses.
"The mugs. How do you suppose they work to keep the coffee hot?" He slurped his hotter than average coffee again and waited for her response.
Gerty sighed, closed her book, and removed her reading glasses. She folded them together and placed them on top of her book on the end table. "Honestly, Gary, must we go over this again?" She had apparently forgotten that she was the one who brought it up not moments ago. And technically the last time they had gone over it was 40 years ago even though she mentioned it often. Gerty did not give Gary any time to respond before going into her explanation of how the mug's shape worked to keep the coffee hotter, longer.
"You understand how a traditional pizza oven is shaped or a fireplace with a smaller opening on top that lets out a small amount of heat, correct?" She looked at Gary as if this had been explained to him over and over again. He replied in the affirmative and she continued. "In the manner that those devices work to maintain high levels of heat, so does this coffee mug. Gerty sipped from her mug with satisfaction having felt confident in her explanation.
Gary allowed Gerty to drink, pick up her book and glasses and continue to read before offering a question in response. He sipped from his own mug again and then asked, "But, Gerty..." He paused so she could stop reading and place her attention on him. And with a sigh, she did. He continued. "Do not a pizza oven and a fireplace require fuel in the form of coal or wood in order to maintain their heat?" Gary could see the agitation in Gerty's mannerisms, but after 40 years of marriage, he knew that under that agitation was the desire to debate and debate was always welcomed at 1500 Hanover Lane.
Gerty took a sip of hot coffee and thought for a moment. Gary noticed a slight smile come across her lips before it disappeared. He knew she had an answer for him that would likely destroy his unthought out question. Even he knew the perfect rebuttal and now figured that she must know it too. Gerty looked at Gary and slowly shook her head. The smile returned. "Gary, I am surprised that you do not know this about pizza ovens. Surely you remember it from the pizza making class we took in Florence."
Gary looked up and to the left, searching for the memory of the experience. This was, of course, for show. He knew exactly what class she was referring to and what fact she had eluded to. He decided to continue playing with her the way he knew she enjoyed. He returned his gaze to her with a confused expression on his face. "Florence, South Carolina?" he asked.
Gerty raised her left hand in the air and threw her head back a bit with a slight roll of the eyes. She shook her head and said, "Gary, you silly old man." Gerty went back to her reading. Still shaking her head.
Gary watched her knowing that she could not leave it at that. She heaved a sigh and removed her glasses. Seeing that, Gary turned to his reading. She looked over to Gary, not caring that he was facing his book and began speaking. "You know very well that a well-designed pizza oven can hold its heat for many hours and a large fraction of its heat for days. So do not insult my intelligence by acting as if you do not remember our time in Firenze, Italy or that these mugs are superior at holding in the heat of our coffee."
Gerty stopped and waited for Gary to lift his head and cede her the point and win for this round. She sipped from her coffee then cleared her throat. Gary looked up from his book and over to Gerty and asked, "I'm sorry, Dear, what was that?"
Gerty pursed her lips and wagged her right index finger at Gary. Then she pointed her finger at him and leaned in to say, "Your book is upside down, Dear."
Chapter 2: Thursday Is Errand Day

“Gary, I do believe that every shopping cart in this establishment is afflicted with at least one malfunctioning wheel.” Gerty looked up from the wobbly wheel on the front of the cart that Gary was pushing down the coffee aisle. The wheel was making quite the racket and Gerty was becoming embarrassed as if the condition of the cart was her responsibility. “Sometimes I feel as if I should be carrying my own can of 3-IN-ONE oil so that I may address any mechanical issues I come across while shopping for my weekly supplies. Perhaps we should indeed venture to aisle 13 and procure a can or two.
Gary listened and pushed as Gerty went on about the matter at hand. Her one sided conversation did not deter her in her shopping duties, however. She could navigate the store with her eyes closed and retrieve every item on their list without making a single mistake. Why they even had a list was a confusing fact for Gary. They had been buying exactly the same items in the same amounts for the past five years. Even still, Gerty carried the two inch wide, ten inch long strip of paper with her every Thursday morning. She held the list in her left hand as she navigated the aisles, walking directly to each item. Though, she would be thrown off her routine when a new store manager would decide to do a redesign.
Andrew, the stock boy, looked up from his squatted position in front of the Frosted Flakes when Gary and Gerty came around the corner into his aisle. He stood with a 12 ounce box in his hand and waited for them to stop in front of him. “Good morning, Mrs. and Mr. Hanover. How are you this fine Thursday?” He placed the box of Frosted Flakes cereal in their cart in the corner closest to Gary’s left hand. Gerty approved with a nod. Andrew stepped back and clasped his hands behind his back. “Is there anything I can help you find?” he asked.
“Not so long as everything on my list is in its proper location.” Before Andrew could tell her that the half-and-half had been moved to the other side of the artificial creamers, she kept on. “What you can do is find some 3-IN-ONE oil and take to silencing these shopping cart wheels. I do believe I would rather have someone following behind me scratching their unkempt fingernails down a black board, Andrew.”
He nodded to show his understanding. “Yes, ma’am, I will talk to Mr. Finnegan about the noisy wheels and see what we can do.”
Showing her exasperation, Gerty shook her head and said, “Andrew, I have told you what you can do about it and that is that. There is no need to involve the store owner in a matter such as this. You are more than capable, I am sure of that. I do not know if your counterpart William is, but you are. I expect some action to be taken post haste.” She began walking down the aisle, a little bit faster than normal since this interaction had delayed her schedule.
“Yes, Mrs. Hanover,” said Andrew. “Enjoy the rest of your day.” 
Gary began to follow Gerty and as he passed Andrew he handed him a one dollar bill that he had folded in his left front pocket. “For the oil if you need it,” he said with a smile.
“Thank you, Mr. Hanover. Take Care.” Andrew pushed the dollar bill into his trouser pocket and went back to stocking the shelf with Frosted Flakes.
Expectations
Gerty stepped to the front of the checkout line so she could watch as each item was scanned and displayed on the cashier’s computer screen. Gary unloaded the cart onto the conveyor belt, cold items first. “Good morning, Mr. and Mrs. Hanover,” said Phyllis who was running the register in lane number one that morning. “Did you find everything okay?”
Gerty looked at Andrew, who was now bagging, then she looked back to Phyllis. “Almost everything. Someone moved the half-and-half to the other side of the sweetened creamers. Now, you have regular milk and cream separated by chemicals. So, I am not clear on the logic there, but at least the half-and-half has not been moved to the bread aisle. Perhaps you have a suggestion form I could fill out about that.” She looked at Andrew and then to Gary and smiled.
Phyllis chuckled and said, “I’m sure Mr. Finnegan would love to see a suggestion like that come through. Be sure to sign your name to it.”
Gerty let out a hearty laugh as she was prone to do at the end of each shopping trip. For some reason, the act of shopping put her in a foul mood. The regular shoppers and employees were familiar with her normal personality so they took her shopping persona in stride.
Phyllis and Andrew joined in on the laugh as Gary looked on with pleasure at the return of his Gerty. Long ago he had suggested that he do the shopping himself or have the groceries delivered, but Gerty would have none of that. She insisted that she enjoyed the exercise and the conversations with the people in her community.
Andrew bagged the groceries in paper bags as usual. No other customers asked to use paper bags, but Mr. Finnegan was always happy to keep them in stock for the Hanovers. They used three bags a week. Mr. Finnegan placed an order for 200 bags every January 2 and when they arrived they were stored at register number one since that was the lane the Hanovers used. 
The cart with the squeaky wheel was loaded with the three crisp brown paper bags and Andrew pushed it out the door following behind Gary and Gerty. The installation of the automatic sensor over the doorway had taken some of the joy out of Gary’s life. He used to enjoy stepping on the ribbed mat with the faded arrow that when depressed would open the door and he would say, ‘after you, madam’ and bow at the waist allowing Gerty to walk through the doorway. Now, they simply walked through.
Gary opened the trunk of their 1996 Chevrolet Caprice. There was enough room in there to fit the entire shopping cart, but all it contained was the original spare tire and an emergency roadside kit that Gary had purchased from a door to door salesman in 1999. He had come to the house foretelling the horrors that Y2K was going to bring. Gary tried to explain that they didn’t have a computer, but the salesman assured him that their car was full of computers and that he was bound to need the kit in the near future. More than 20 years had passed and the kit had not been opened since the salesman’s presentation. Gerty had told Gary there was no need for the kit because they had the auto club membership, but it was too late. Gary had already signed the purchase agreement and the salesman was long gone.
“Thank you, Andrew. Put them anywhere,” said Gerty as she stood at the rear of the car waiting for the grocery bags to be loaded. Andrew removed each bag one by one from the shopping cart and placed them in the trunk with care. The bag with the eggs and the bread was placed by the bag with the tomato soup and peanut butter which was held in place by the bag that contained the milk, half-and-half, and orange juice.
Andrew closed the trunk lid. “There you go. You’re all set,” he said without moving away. Gerty had always given him a tip for helping them to their car, even though as she had pointed out, the help was not needed but was accepted as customary. She thanked Andrew and handed him a silver dollar explaining to him that she had received it as change from Ronald at the service station earlier that morning.
Andrew said thank you and started away, pushing the squeaky cart back to the store. Gerty turned and called to him, “Never mind about those wheels, Andrew. I shall use them as a reminder of what is good in life.”
He smiled and nodded then turned back to his duty of gathering stray carts on his way back to the building. Gary stood at the side of the car holding the door open for Gerty. When she turned back toward the car he said, “My lady,” and motioned for her to enter the car.
“Thank you, my good man, “ she said as she entered and sat in the large leather passenger seat. They had chosen this car because of its size and power. There was enough room on the inside for six grown men to ride comfortably across the entire state of Texas without ever needing to stop for a stretch.
Chapter 3: What Kind Of Rut?
Hanover Lane was a lane for sure. It was no street, no avenue, no boulevard. One home sat on Hanover Lane. That’s all there ever had been and all there ever will be. Gary parked the Caprice in the carriage house which was detached from the residence and a good thirty paces from the kitchen door. The kitchen was an addition to the house, added in the 1950s and that is where the style and decor remained. Gary and Gerty had no reason to remodel. Everything was functional and because of the large appliances’ build quality and simple design, they were easy to maintain. Ernie, the repair man, after much searching had always been able to find the needed parts.
Gary unloaded the groceries, removing them one by one placing them on the counter top while Gerty put them away in their proper location. “Milk was priced 15 cents more this week, Gary.” She always watched the prices of every item they bought even though she didn’t have to. They had enough money to cover their needs, plus a little bit more.
“I saw that,” said Gary who also knew the price of every item. “But the bread was a quarter lower. So I guess the house doesn’t always win. I’m sure Mr. Finnegan will get wise to it at some point and bring balance back to the shelves of Finnegan’s Family Grocery.” Gary folded the paper bags and placed them in the cupboard at his feet.
“Gary, I believe you would never speak if a laugh was not possible. But, you have said that same thing before about Mr. Finnegan. You need some new material.” Gerty finished putting away the dry goods which took but a moment.
Gary thought about what Gerty had said. He agreed with her, but he got his material from life experiences and they hadn’t had any new experiences in quite some time. “Gerty.”
She was standing at the coffee maker preparing their mid-morning coffee. “What is it, Gary?” She continued with her task, but listened as he spoke.
Gary wanted to phrase his question properly so as to not place blame of any kind. They had spoken in the past about routine and annoying deviations, but he thought it was time to discuss it again. “Are we in a rut?” he asked, leaning back against the counter.
Gerty stopped scooping the coffee and turned to face Gary. She considered for a moment and then responded. “Well, Gary, if you mean to ask if we are physically in a track worn by a wheel, I would say no. If you are asking if we are like male deer, I would say no. However, if you are asking if we are in a monotonous routine that is dull and unproductive, I might be inclined to take offense.” She stopped Gary from interjecting and then continued. “As I was saying, I might be inclined to take offense, if I disagreed. But Gary, I do not disagree. I believe we are in a routine that can sometimes seem dull, however, I am not sure what to do about it at this stage of life.”
Gary was reassured by her answer, but he too did not know what to do about it. They both knew that they preferred to stay home over attending a party. When they attended parties, (this was a rare occurrence) they tended to congregate with each other in a corner, discussing the books they were reading or commenting on how fashion had changed and stayed the same all at once. Occasionally someone would join them for a few moments of chat about the party and the food. Of course, politics would come up but the last time Gary and Gerty had voted, Nixon had been elected. Unlike many topics of discussion, they could speak only in generalities, but this seemed to suffice. Apparently the more things change the more they stay the same. 
“I’m glad to hear you feel the same way, Gerty. I have given it some thought but I don’t really know where to begin. What are people our age doing?”
Gerty replied matter of factly. “Dying, Gary. People our age are dying.” She turned around and scooped one more tablespoon of coffee into the filter basket then closed the lid and toggled the switch on the coffee maker.
“Oh, Gerty, that’s not true. The life expectancy for a female in Texas is 81.1 years and 75.9 years for a male. We still have plenty of time here.” Gary had done some research because he wanted to know what more to expect out of life and he decided that he wanted some adventure in the next 10 years of his life.
“Gary, that’s not fair. You are not going to leave me here alone to do the shopping.” They had a history of making jokes back and forth about who was going to die first and what that would mean for the other. They joked about life insurance money (there was none), new young spouses, and a Romeo and Juliet ending. “On the other hand, I would save money by not having to buy cereal and milk. You do eat like a small child sometimes. Perhaps you could remove yourself from the rut of eating cereal.”
“Now that, Gerty, is something I will continue even after I die. I’m sure there must be cereal in Heaven.”
“Watching and listening to you eat your Frosted Flakes can be quite torturous. I hope for the sake of your next wife, you give it up.”
Gary and Gerty enjoyed this witty banter and each interaction drew them closer to each other and put them more in love, even after 40 years. People who knew them would sometimes comment on their exchanges, especially when displayed in public. At a town meeting, several years before this time, Gary stood to address the council to complain about the old lady who lived on Hanover Lane. The council allowed this to go one for all of one minute before calling order to the meeting. The mayor apologized to the new members of the town (a young couple who had moved from Austin to get away from the crazy city life) and explained the situation and that theatrics was a specialty of Mr. and Mrs. Hanover. The young couple thought it was endearing and it helped them feel at home.
“Gerty, you know I would never remarry. Why would I do that to myself?”
The coffee maker had finished brewing and Gerty had stopped listening to Gary so she could prepare the mugs. She poured the coffee and turned to Gary. “What was it we were discussing?” she asked. Neither he nor she could recall that they had been discussing the rut they were in. At that moment, the small clock on the window sill above the sink beeped its reminder. “It makes no matter,” said Gerty, “It is time for our 11:30 coffee.”
The beep and the comment reminded Gary what they had been discussing, but he held onto his comments on the subject. Now that he knew she felt the same way, he wanted to come up with some ideas on what they could do to change up the pace. “That it is, Gerty.” He picked up their mugs and followed her into the den where they sat in their favorite chairs, drinking the same coffee they had been drinking for seven years.
Chapter 4

Gary had started squeezing the toothpaste from the bottom of the tube a few years prior, after the toothpaste tube itself offered the suggestion, For best results, squeeze tube from the bottom and flatten as you go up. This was after years of Gerty attempting to explain the benefits of squeezing from the bottom. She had said that it would make him a more organized person. He had told her that he didn’t need to be organized because he had her.
Gerty walked into the bathroom while Gary was brushing his teeth. She had an idea and was anxious to share it with Gary even though this was not normally the time they would discuss things. “Gary, I have a brilliant idea in relation to what we were discussing earlier today before coffee. Do you remember? About being in a rut?”
He remembered. He had been thinking about it most of the day. Gary was excited to hear that she had an idea she was willing to share. “What is it?” he asked after spitting in the sink.
She handed him a hand towel and began. “It really is quite brilliant. I am surprised to only now be thinking of it.” She paused for effect.
Gary interjected in his excitement, “Well, what is it? You’ve got me on cacti and quills.” They had started saying this instead of ‘pins and needles’ some years before when they visited a zoo in the desert. The director of the zoo was a friend from college and the person who had introduced Gary and Gerty. When they had been invited to the grand opening, they knew they must go.
Gerty chuckled and continued. “We shall start a book club.” Gary reminded her that they had joined a book club before and that it was simply awful. No one spoke intelligently about the book and he was the lone man in attendance. Gerty went on. “I understand all of that and this is why I am suggesting we start our own. We can have the meeting here and control who is allowed to attend, what books will be read and discussed and what day of the week it will be held. We can control all of it, Gary.”
Gary considered this while he flossed his teeth. He remembered well when Gerty had had ideas similar to this in the past. Of course things don’t always go as planned when including other people. He thought this could be different, but he wanted to be realistic. “Do you remember the supper club?”
“Now, Gary, you know very well that I remember the supper club, but that is altogether different. Those people were interested only in eating and talking about other people. That is all. I am talking about something completely new and in our control. Before we move any further, you must understand this.”
Gary was interested in trying out something new and he did enjoy reading and discussing the books and the ideas within the books. “Perhaps it could work if we set it up properly. What are you thinking exactly?” They both walked out of the bathroom and into the hall.
“Do you need anything from the kitchen?” asked Gerty while she considered what her thoughts were in regards to the book club specifics. Gary replied in the negative and Gerty decided that she didn’t need anything either. They continued down the hall to the bedroom where they walked in and Gary closed the door behind them. Gerty continued. “To begin with, we could have it on Tuesday evenings at seven. Each week, we will discuss a new book of our choosing. We will not serve any food. I do not want people discussing Hemingway with a mouth full of saltine crackers. The mouth shrapnel alone would be the cause for a revolt by the other guests. No, we will serve decaffeinated coffee and maybe tea if anyone requests it.”
Gary had heard Gerty say ‘to begin with’, but it appeared to him that she had the event completely planned from beginning to end. He did not agree with the idea of no food, but did agree that saltine crackers should not be made available. With no food being served he felt as though he himself would avoid attending. How could they expect anyone else to attend? “Maybe, Gerty, we could serve some kind of food that doesn’t produce debris. I believe the lack of food entirely could mean a quick end to the meeting and any subsequent meetings. What about serving dried fruits? Raisins? Prunes?”
Gerty interrupted, “Heavens, no. Not prunes. They are far too large to eat in one bite without having to keep one’s mouth agape. They cause issues with dentures and bridgework. Oh! And let us not forget that we have but one bathroom. No. Prunes are out of the question. Raisins, we can work with. It is settled. We will serve raisins and coffee.”
“And tea by request. Don’t forget.” Gary wondered what the response would be to an invitation for a book club where raisins and coffee were advertised. Small print in italics at the bottom Tea by request.
“So right. I shall get started on planning in the morning.” Gerty was so excited that she took off her robe, climbed into bed, and picked up her notebook to begin making a list of who she might invite.
***
Gary awaked to find that Gerty had gotten out of bed early and he could see that the light in the hall was on. He walked to the den to find Gerty sitting in her wingback chair holding her pen and notebook. “What do you have there?” he asked as he sat down in his chair with his mug of coffee.
“Good morning, Gary.” She set her notebook on her lap and picked up her coffee mug. “As you well know we are hosting a weekly book club starting on Tuesday and I have started to compile a list of potential invitees.” She tapped her notebook.
Gary swallowed some coffee and set his mug on the end table. He was taken by surprise that she had compiled a list of guests already. She had yet to consult with Mildred, the librarian, or Bethany at the bookshop. “Mm, may I see the list?” He held out his hand.
Gerty set her coffee down and held the notebook between her hands as if she were going to read from it. She looked down at it and then to Gary. “There is a slight problem, I’m afraid.” She pulled the notebook to her chest in an effort to conceal the contents of its pages.
Perhaps she has made the list too large, thought Gary, and the problem was that their modest home could not accommodate such a gathering. Now they would have to work on whittling down the number of guests in an effort to keep from offending anyone whom they did not include. “I’m sure whatever the problem is, we can sort it out. Please may I see your list?”
Gerty pulled the notebook from her chest, looked at it again before handing it across the end table to Gary. He took the notebook in his hands and moved it into his line of sight. Gary pushed the notebook away then pulled it in trying to bring it into focus. While maintaining his grip with his right hand, he held out his left toward Gerty who then placed the temple of her reading glasses into his hand. After donning the glasses he put his attention on the notebook. He examined it for a moment before lowering it into his lap and removing the reading glasses. He looked at Gerty with a furrowed brow. She looked almost ashamed but maintained eye contact with him. “Gerty,” he said.
She threw up her hands. “I know. I know. You don’t even have to say it. I do not know what came over me. I am not even sure I had control of the pen. Perhaps that is it! Perhaps it was a possession.” Gerty lowered her head and slowly shook it.
Gary considered a moment and looked back at the notebook. “A possession? What could have possessed you? I do have one question. Did you write down all these names before crossing them out or did you do it one at a time? And when did you add the notes next to each name?”
Gerty reached out and took the notebook from Gary. She chuckled. “Well, if you must know, I wrote down all of the names before crossing them out. Some of them, though, did have notes next to them prior to being crossed out.”
Gary returned the chuckle and asked, “What about the note next to Ronald’s name? Was that added before or after you decided to not invite him to the book club meeting?”
Gerty’s face tinged with red due to a slight case of embarrassment coming on. “That particular note was added prior to his name being lined through. One can never tell when having a lush at a gathering would be good or bad. I ultimately decided against it in this case. However, if the book club needs some flair added, then he may receive an invitation in the future.”
Gary had always thought party planning brought out the worst in Gerty. The reason being that she did not actually want to have any parties. Having a few guests here and there was always welcomed, but large numbers did not agree with either of them. “Perhaps we should put a hold on the book club at this point in time. Is it really something you feel up to?”
Gerty looked at her notebook in her hands and considered Gary’s remarks. She flipped the book over, but nothing had been written on that side. Laying the notebook on the end table, she said, “I believe I want to do something to break up our routine, but you may be right.” She tore the page of uninvited guests from her notebook and leaned forward to place it in the fire. Gary and Gerty watched the paper burn into ashes before either of them spoke.
It was Gary who broke the silence. “So, now that that’s behind us.” That was all he had. They both picked up their coffee mugs and the books they were reading. Silence sat between them until a flipped page stirred the air.
Chapter 5
Visits to the bookstore and the library alternated on Thursday mornings between visits to the service station and the market. The bank opened at eight and was always the first stop. That Thursday was the library’s turn. “Has anything new come in since our last visit, Mildred?” asked Gerty in a whisper at the circulation desk. 
Mildred pushed back her chair to a set of rolling bookcases. She ran her finger along a row of books on the second shelf. Touching the top of a book and pivoting it toward her she removed it and returned to the desk. Mildred showed Gary and Gerty the cover of the book which they both read silently. “It’s new and she’s a promising fiction writer with a successful track record in non-fiction. I believe you’ll enjoy it.” She scanned the book into their account as a check out without them needing to ask her to. They always enjoyed her recommendations.
Gary took the book from Mildred and placed it on the selection of books they had gathered from the stacks. “I think this should do us for the time being,” he whispered. “We’re trying to get out of our rut.”
Gerty would have been embarrassed had Gary said this to anyone else, but she had known Mildred for three decades and considered her a friend. This fact hadn’t kept Gerty from crossing through Mildred’s name and writing ‘likes cats’ next to it. Mildred did more than like cats. Mildred owned many cats. At last count, there were 13 that Mildred knew of. It had started 27 years earlier with one cat named Whiskers. Well, Mildred had said Whiskers needed a friend and before Mildred knew it, Whiskers and her friend were more than friends and the number of cats grew from there. To this day, Mildred does not trust Elaine McGrath, the seven years old who gave to Mildred Whisker’s friend who had supposedly been fixed. Elaine is 34 years old now and still lives in town. Mildredn leaves the room when Elaine brings her children into the library.
“If you are really trying to get out of a rut,” said Mildred, “you need to look at the bulletin board in the vestibule. Patrons are always posting about events and things for sale or groups to join. And to my vexation, they fail to remove the expired bills of advertisement.” Mildred handed the due date receipt to Gary and wished them well.
“Thank you for the recommendation, Mildred, on both accounts. We shall look at the postings on the board. We will see you in two week’s time.” Gerty motioned for Gary to walk on.
They approached the board and stood side by side staring blankly at the colorful display. “I suppose we should examine it systematically,” said Gary. He thought the 32 square foot board could be broken into sections and they could read each section separately, bringing to the attention of the other something of interest.
“We don’t have time for that Gary. We’ve used extra time conversing with Mildred already and we still need to get to the market by 10.” There was no need for her to look at her watch because her inner clock had always been more accurate.
Gary added his thoughts on their timetable. “Perhaps we don’t need to get to the market by 10. It doesn’t close until 6 today and we don’t have any special appointments today.” He stepped to the right corner of the board and began reading while Gerty digested his statement.
“We always go to the market at 10 on Thursdays, Gary. I am suggesting we get out of a rut, not completely dismantle the fabric of our being in one fell swoop. I believe we need to have a conversation about our next steps if we are to be on the same page.” She looked up at her area of the board.

“I’ll show you when I come down and I am coming down as soon as I stack these boxes back up.” Gary reached down to pick up the documents box and when he heaved it up, the bottom fell out of it and the documents flopped onto the attic floor. “Oh, drat! What a mess.” Gary stared at the mess of papers on the ground and thought about what to do. Gerty must not have heard, he thought. He considered for a moment more. He reminded himself that Gerty never came into the attic so she would never know about the mess. He didn’t care that the papers were stored on the floor instead of in a box. They’re not going anywhere. 
Gary decided to leave everything where it was. He turned off the light and descended the attic stairs, bypassing the broken step. He bent down and was lifting the bottom portion of the stairs when Gerty walked into the hallway. “Wait! Keep those down,” she said.
Gary held his hands on the section of stairs and kept looking straight at them to avoid making eye contact with Gerty. He shut his eyes and sighed to himself. “Why? We’ve got everything down that we need from up there.” He continued the operation of folding the stairs.
“Gary, please. I believe there is something in the other box that would complete my ensemble. Leave the steps down and I will go up and look for it.” She stepped forward to nudge Gary aside.
“No!” said Gary as he spun around and grabbed Gerty’s shoulders. “You can’t go up there. I’ll go and get it. What is it? I can find it.” Beads of  sweat appeared on Gary’s brow as he spoke and waited for Gerty’s response.
“What has gotten into you, Gary? You are sweating and stammering. Did you hit your head when that step broke?” Gerty used her index finger to pull down the skin under Gary’s right eye so she could examine his pupil.
He pushed her hand away from his face and defending himself said, “No, nothing is wrong. I just want to get the thing for you from the attic.”
Gerty was surprised by Gary’s curt attitude and could tell that he was either hiding something or had been injured. “Gary, I feel you may have a concussion and I would like for you to sit down. I’ll go into the attic to look for the item.”
Gary let her pass because he did not know what to say. She pulled down the lower portion of the steps and let it rest on the floor. As she stepped up on to the first step, Gary blurted out, “There’s mold!”
Gerty stopped and turned to look over her shoulder at Gary. “What do you mean, there’s mold?”
Gary reached out his hand to help Gerty off the ladder, but she refused it. “In the attic. Mold is in the attic.” He regretted immediately what he had said.
“Mold?”
He knew he had to turn around on this path of deceit or it would begin to widen, he would get lost and end up in destruction. “I mean there could be mold and you don’t need to go up there. It’s bad for your lungs. You remember what the doctor said about your lungs?”
“Yes, he said that my lungs are stronger than your lungs. Regardless, if there’s mold up there we should…” At the moment Gerty had said ‘Regardless’ the air conditioning unit had turned on. It was an unseasonably warm day. The return vent was located next to the attic opening and when it started drawing in air it pulled from the attic which moved the air, along with the papers that had fallen. A few loose papers fluttered through the attic opening and fell to the ground as Gary and Gerty watched.
Gary lifted his eyes from the ground and met Gerty’s glare. She knows, he thought. His eyes widened and he spoke. “So, what happened was…” Gerty turned and began climbing the steps. “...there’s a box of papers…”
Gerty’s head reached the top and she took over the explanation. “A box of papers that you spilled everywhere and planned on leaving a mess.” She looked down on Gary. “Mold. You ought to be ashamed of yourself. How could you lie to me to protect yourself from having to clean up a few papers? What else are you lying about? Is Gary your real name? Where were you born? Did you really pull that man from that burning van?”
Gary hung his head. He felt a real kind of shame. Gary shook his head then looked up at Gerty.
Gerty shook her head, turned around and climbed down the attic stairs. She took Gary’s face in her hands. “ Do not ever lie to me again.” Gary shook his head with a little help from Gerty’s hands. “If you are going to lie, do it on the stage.” Gerty looked at her watch then threw her hands in the air. “We have no time for this. We will be late if we do not leave now.”
Gary was relieved that there was no time for further discussion of his deception, but they had also used time that had been necessary to properly prepare. “What about our costumes?”
“We shall audition out of costume. It is not my desired way, but it will have to suffice. Surely, we will still be the best performers for the roles.” Gerty walked away from Gary and toward the bedroom, speaking as she walked, “Close the attic steps, Gary. You can clean up later.”
“Yes, Dear.” Gary slid the costume pieces and the papers to the wall with his foot. He folded the ladder and grabbed the string then nudged the wood to give the springs the go-ahead to do their work of pulling the door closed. They squeaked and popped and the door sealed the attic off from the hallway. Gary sighed and turned to go to the bedroom where he would pick up his wallet and keys so they could make their way to the theater.

Gary pulled the long Caprice into the theater parking lot 25 minutes before the auditions were scheduled to be held. He chose a space near the far end of the lot so their car would be protected from the ‘reckless driving of young actors,’ as he had put it when Gerty had asked.
They were alone in the parking lot. Gary rolled the windows down and turned off the ignition. He put his arm on the sill and his fingers tapped the side of the car near the side view mirror. “First ones here,” he said.
Gerty looked around the lot and then at her watch. Then back around the lot. “Yes, but why? The auditions open in 20 minutes. Where is everyone?” She looked at her watch again, a sign that she was nervous.
Gary pursed his lips and looked around the lot himself. He turned the key in the ignition to see the time on the radio. “Yep, 18 minutes to go.” He turned the key back.
Gerty looked at him with confusion wondering why he didn’t seem concerned. “Right. Eighteen minutes. People are not that busy are they? Or that disorganized?” She looked back around at the parking lot. A small blue Honda pulled into the lot. “Oh! Well, there’s one car now.”
Gary turned to look and nodded. He returned front and said, “Maybe theater is not as popular as it used to be. “He continued tapping his fingers on the door and bobbing his head to some nonexistent music.
Still looking at the blue Honda, Gerty said, “They’re simply sitting in there.”
Gary looked over at Gerty. “Who?”
“The people in the blue car. They’re just sitting there. What are they doing?”
Gary looked at the blue car then back to Gerty. “They’re probably waiting, like us.”
“Right. Right. How silly of me.” Gerty swung back around to face front. She checked her watch again, but said nothing. She sighed and began tapping on her purse.
Gary continued his window drumming. Gerty checked her watch again. “Thirteen minutes.” Gary said nothing. She checked the parking lot again to find the lone blue Honda and its driver and passenger. She frowned and faced back to the front. Her tapping became more rapid and her checks of the parking lot more frequent. She looked at Gary who seemed unconcerned. “Six minutes, Gary. Something is wrong. Where is everyone else?” Before Gary could respond, Gerty saw the blue car occupants emerge. “Oh wait, they are going towards the theater.” Gary looked over to see for himself. Gerty continued, “Let’s go, Gary.” She opened her own door and got out of the car.
Gary rushed to get the windows up and get himself out of the car so he could catch up with Gerty. He reached her before she made it to the theater door. From behind, they approached a young man and woman who were unlocking the door.
“Good evening,” said Gerty startling them. She was a bit of a sidler and she never wore shoes that made noise.
They spun around with wide eyes and surprised expressions. The man was holding the keys and appeared to be in charge, but the woman responded. “Oh, hi. What can we do for you?”
Gerty was a bit annoyed by the question because the answer was blindingly obvious to her. They could open the door so Gerty and Gary could audition and change the face of the town’s theater scene.  Gerty knew, though, that this could be the director so she kept her sarcasm to herself. “We are here to audition for Fiddler on The Roof. I will be auditioning for the role of Golde and my husband,” she pointed back at Gary with her upturned flat palm, “Tevye.”
The woman grimaced and looked back at the man who said, “Ooh, I’m sorry, but that show has been cancelled. We posted about the cancellation on the website and we put out a few flyers announcing it. I’m so sorry you’ve wasted your time.”
Gerty considered for a moment then looked at Gary who shrugged his shoulders. She looked back at the man. “We did see flyers announcing the auditions, but none announcing the cancellation. Where did you post those flyers?” She shifted her weight to one leg and placed her hands on her hips.
“Well, we uh, put one up here.” He pointed to the window of the enclosed case with the bulletin board inside; the one that Gerty and Gary had decided to not check since they knew it would be locked. “And, let’s see, we put one up at my shop, Inked Expressions. It’s a tattoo parlor downtown. We’ve been there a few years.”
Gary and Gerty knew the place well. They had opposed its opening vehemently at a town hall meeting. They had said that it would bring in all sorts of riff raff. However, over the years it had organized popular community events and charity drives.
The man continued, “And, of course, the website like I mentioned. Again, I’m sorry you folks didn’t hear about it. Is there anything else I can do for you?” He raised his eyebrows and smiled.
Both Gary and Gerty were at a loss. They had gone through all of that trouble to orchestrate the removal of those flyers to help their chances at getting the roles. Gary had enjoyed the time and the adventure, but Gerty was upset at their wasted efforts. Since she was no longer concerned about offending this man who was likely the director, she told him what she was thinking.
“Well, it would have been good of you to remove the flyers that announced the auditions so that people like us could have avoided this situation.” She was well aware that other people had apparently learned of the cancellation since there was nobody else there.
“Yes, I know and again I’m sorry. I had forgotten about those flyers until this morning, but when I went to remove them I only found a few still in place. I’m not sure when they were removed, but it was obviously after you had seen one. I do hope this situation won’t keep you away from the theater in the future.” He looked down at this watch and back up at Gerty and Gary.
Gerty’s anger was being redirected at herself and Gary for their immature plot. Why did we ever do such a thing, she thought. She flipped a switch on her attitude toward the man. “No, no. No worries. We are sorry to have kept you.” She turned to Gary. “Let’s go, Dear.”
They all said parting pleasantries and Gary and Gerty walked to their car. Gary held the door for Gerty as she got in and sat down placing her purse on her lap. Gary walked around the back end of the car, checking for the scratch from the pole in the bank parking lot but finding nothing. He got in the driver’s seat, closed his door and buckled up. He started the car and sighed. Gary looked over to Gerty and asked, “Well, Dear.” She looked at him. He continued. “It’s Friday and the night is young. What would you like to do?”
A friendly smile grew on her face. She moved her left hand and placed it on Gary’s hand which was resting on the top of the bench seat back. He returned the smile. She breathed in and said, “Well, my love, you do have that pile of documents to clean up in the attic.”
